entry.title: D-Day’s First Battle | The British Airborne’s Fight for Pegasus Bridge

media:group.media:title: D-Day’s First Battle | The British Airborne’s Fight for Pegasus Bridge
media:group.media:description:
The Battle for Pegasus Bridge, D-Day, 6 June 1944. At sixteen minutes past midnight, six Horsa gliders came down in silence beside two bridges east of Sword Beach - the Caen Canal crossing at Bénouville and the swing bridge over the River Orne at Ranville. The 181 men of D Company, 2nd Ox and Bucks Light Infantry, under Major John Howard had one job: take both bridges intact before the Germans could blow them, and hold until relieved. If the bridges fell, the 21st Panzer Division could roll into the flank of the invasion; if they were destroyed, the whole 6th Airborne Division would be stranded east of the water. It was the first fight of D-Day, and it opened with the first British soldier killed on French soil.
This animated map account of Pegasus Bridge follows the coup de main from the first crash landing to the relief 24 hours later: Lieutenant Den Brotheridge's charge across the canal bridge and his death at the far end; Lieutenant Sandy Smith crossing on a wrecked knee; the engineers hunting through the girders for charges that were never fitted; Lieutenant Dennis Fox's platoon taking the Orne bridge with a single mortar round; Sergeant Wagger Thornton's one PIAT shot that stopped the German armour at the junction; 7 Para's fight for Bénouville and Le Port through the morning; the gunboats from Ouistreham; Private Wally Parr's captured anti-tank gun; and Bill Millin piping Lord Lovat's commandos in from the sea - Brigadier Nigel Poett, Lieutenant Colonel Geoffrey Pine-Coffin, Major Nigel Taylor, Private Michael McGee, Corporal Tommy Killeen, and Georges Gondrée, whose café became the first house in France to be liberated.

entry.title: The Battle of Juno Beach D-Day 1944 | Canada's Longest Day (Animated)

media:group.media:title: The Battle of Juno Beach D-Day 1944 | Canada's Longest Day (Animated)
media:group.media:description:
The Battle of Juno Beach, D-Day, 6 June 1944. At dawn on D-Day, the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division stormed Juno Beach — eight kilometres of Normandy seafront between the British beaches at Gold and Sword, where three quiet resort towns had been turned into fortresses. Courseulles-sur-Mer, Bernières-sur-Mer and Saint-Aubin-sur-Mer hid German guns in four feet of concrete, sighted along the sand, untouched by the naval bombardment. The Canadian objective on D-Day: take the three towns, push ten miles inland, and cut the road between Caen and Bayeux before nightfall.
This animated map documentary of the Battle of Juno Beach follows the Normandy landings through the units that fought them: the Royal Winnipeg Rifles and the DD tanks of the 1st Hussars against the dune fortress of WN 31; the Regina Rifles' block-by-block clearance of Courseulles against the most heavily fortified position on the Anglo-Canadian front; the Queen's Own Rifles' landing into the guns of WN 28 at Bernières and the storming of the seawall; the Régiment de la Chaudière's fight for the exit at Les Perrucques; the North Shore Regiment and the Fort Garry Horse against the hidden gun that held Saint-Aubin; and the drive inland that carried the Canadians deeper into France than any division in the Allied invasion — Captain Philip Gower, Lieutenant Bill Grayson, the Dalton brothers, Lieutenant Bill Herbert, Lieutenant Moisan, and Lieutenant Bill McCormick's three Shermans on the Caen–Bayeux railway.

entry.title: The Battle of Saint-Lô 1944 | Hill 192, Normandy Bocage & the Major of St-Lô (Animated - No AI)

media:group.media:title: The Battle of Saint-Lô 1944 | Hill 192, Normandy Bocage & the Major of St-Lô (Animated - No AI)
media:group.media:description:
The Battle of Saint-Lô, July 1944. Six weeks after D-Day, the Allied advance through Normandy had stalled in the bocage - hedgerow country where every field was a fortress and every advance was paid for by the yard. To break out of Normandy, the American First Army needed Saint-Lô, the road junction of lower Normandy and the springboard for Operation Cobra.
This animated map documentary follows the battle through the units that fought it: the 30th Infantry Division's defence of the Vire bridgehead against the Panzer Lehr Division; the 2nd Infantry Division's assault on Hill 192 against the paratroopers of the 3rd Fallschirmjäger Division; the 29th Infantry Division's drive down the Martinville Ridge and the rescue of the Lost Battalion at La Madeleine; the 134th Infantry, 35th Division at Hill 122; and Task Force C's entry into the ruined town on 18 July 1944 - led by Brigadier General Norman Cota, and carrying the body of Major Thomas Howie, the Major of Saint-Lô.

entry.title: The 101st Airborne's Assault on Carentan | Cole's Charge & Bloody Gulch (Animated)

media:group.media:title: The 101st Airborne's Assault on Carentan | Cole's Charge & Bloody Gulch (Animated)
media:group.media:description:
In June 1944, a single raised causeway across flooded marsh was the only road into Carentan — the town that locked the gap between Utah and Omaha beaches. This is the 101st Airborne's assault on Carentan: the eight-day fight to take the town and hold it, from Cole's Charge on the causeway to the stand at Bloody Gulch.
From the light tank burning at Dead Man's Corner, to Lieutenant Colonel Robert Cole's bayonet charge across the meadow, to the 17th SS counterattack at Bloody Gulch, the paratroopers of the 502nd and 506th and the glidermen of the 327th secured the link between the two American beachheads — and held it against everything the Germans sent back.
This is also the full operational context behind the Carentan chapter of Band of Brothers: Richard Winters, Easy Company, and the stand at Bloody Gulch, set inside the multi-regiment battle they were one part of.
Iron Breach — cinematic, animated top-down battle-map documentaries of the European campaign, told at the level of the men who fought it. "Telling the stories of men who died for those they would never meet."

entry.title: Rangers Lead the Way: The D-Day Assault on Pointe du Hoc and Omaha Beach | Animated Documentary

media:group.media:title: Rangers Lead the Way: The D-Day Assault on Pointe du Hoc and Omaha Beach | Animated Documentary
media:group.media:description:
On June 6, 1944, Lieutenant Colonel James Rudder led 225 Rangers up the cliffs of Pointe du Hoc — scaling rope ladders under fire to destroy six heavy guns threatening both American invasion beaches. When they reached the top, the casemates were empty.
This is the full story of the U.S. Army Rangers on D-Day: the cliff assault at Pointe du Hoc, the desperate fighting on Omaha Beach, and the 48-hour battle to hold what they had taken — outnumbered, cut off, and waiting for a relief that came almost too late.
Featuring the 2nd and 5th Ranger Battalions, Brigadier General Norman Cota's charge across Omaha Beach, and First Sergeant Leonard Lomell's patrol that found — and destroyed — the missing guns. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🎖️ CHAPTERS 0:00:00 Introduction 0:00:40 The Plan: Rudder's Three Forces 0:01:59 The Crossing — Navigation Error 0:04:09 Goranson at Charlie Beach 0:05:37 Assault on Pointe du Hoc 0:08:51 Schneider Diverts to Omaha 0:09:41 Dog Green: The Killing Ground 0:10:11 Cota and the 5th Rangers 0:11:16 The Sunken Road 0:12:38 Cut Off: No Reinforcements 0:12:54 The Fight to Hold Pointe du Hoc 0:14:38 Relief: June 8th
